title: One Creator God: What Christians and Muslims Actually Agree On
summary: The real theological common ground between the Christian and Islamic understanding of God, before the differences covered later in this collection.

body.text: The same God, described with real overlap

As covered in Stage 1, Muslims believe "Allah" is simply the word for the same one Creator God worshipped by Abraham, Moses, and Jesus — not a separate deity. Beyond that starting point, the actual description of God in Christian and Islamic teaching overlaps significantly: one all-powerful Creator, all-knowing, all-merciful, eternal, who created the universe out of nothing and to whom every person is ultimately accountable.

Both traditions describe God as just and merciful at once, as hearing prayer, as intervening in human history through prophets and revelation, and as caring about how people treat one another — not a distant, uninvolved force. The 99 Names of Allah in Islamic tradition (Al-Rahman, the Most Merciful; Al-Adl, the Just; Al-Khaliq, the Creator, and so on) would sound, in translation, largely familiar to a Christian's own vocabulary for describing God's character.

body.translation: He is Allah, the Creator, the Inventor, the Fashioner; to Him belong the best names. Whatever is in the heavens and earth is exalting Him.

body.text: Mainstream Christianity describes itself as strictly monotheistic too — one God, not several. This matters for a revert to know clearly: the disagreement covered in the next lesson isn't over whether there is one God versus many; it's over how that one God's nature is understood, specifically the doctrine of the Trinity. Getting this distinction right avoids a common, unhelpful framing — that Islam simply "believes in one God" while Christianity doesn't — which isn't accurate and isn't how most Christians would describe their own belief.
Why naming the agreement matters for you

When a Christian family member fears you've adopted some entirely foreign belief system, it can help to be able to say plainly: the God you're now worshipping is described, in Islam, with real continuity to what you already believed about God's oneness, power, mercy, and justice. The specific and genuine disagreement is narrower than "different God" — and naming that accurately tends to lower the emotional temperature of these conversations.

body.question: Do Muslims and Christians worship a different God, then?
body.answer: Mainstream Islamic teaching says no — Muslims worship the same Creator God that Abraham, Moses, and Jesus worshipped and taught others to worship, described in Arabic as Allah. Where the traditions genuinely diverge is on specific claims about that God's nature (the Trinity) and how He has revealed Himself, not on whether it's the same Being.

body.question: Some Christians insist Allah is a different, specifically Islamic deity — how should I respond?
body.answer: It can help to note that Allah is simply the Arabic word for God, used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews for centuries before Islam and continuing today — it isn't a proper name invented by or exclusive to Muslims, the same way "Dieu," "Gott," and "God" aren't different beings in French, German, and English.

body.question: Before this lesson, how much overlap did you already assume existed between the Christian and Islamic understanding of God?
